title: Turning Panic Into a Plan: DP2 Mid-Fall Check-In
summary: Turn DP2 mid-fall panic into a realistic IB plan for coursework, revision, deadlines, sleep, and weekly priorities from September to November.
body_markdown:
By the middle of the **IB DP2 fall term** , it can feel as though every deadline has become urgent. The solution is not to work on everything simultaneously. Turning panic into a plan mid-fall means identifying what is genuinely time-sensitive, converting large obligations into clear next actions, and maintaining enough revision that DP1 knowledge remains accessible.


This September-to-November check-in explains how to audit deadlines, prioritize coursework, begin sustainable exam preparation, and build a realistic weekly system. It is written mainly for students preparing for a May examination session, although the method works with other school calendars.


### Why DP2 pressure rises during the fall term


DP2 combines several workloads: remaining syllabus content, internal assessments, the Extended Essay, TOK, CAS, university applications, tests, and mock examinations. These responsibilities matter, but they do not have equal urgency.


Coursework deadlines are often close and fixed, while final examinations are important but further away. The aim is to protect both. The IB uses internal and external assessment, with written examinations forming the basis of assessment in most subjects, as explained in its[official assessment overview](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/) .


### Start with a complete DP2 status audit


Spend 30 minutes collecting accurate information before making a timetable. Planning from memory is unreliable because anxiety magnifies vague obligations and hides specific tasks.


List:


- Every IA and its current stage
- Your EE status, feedback, and next deadline
- Your next TOK milestone
- Outstanding CAS records or school requirements
- Tests, oral assessments, and mocks
- University and personal commitments


For each item, record its **deadline** , **current status** , **next physical action** , and **estimated time** . “Work on Biology IA” is vague. “Create two processed-data graphs and explain uncertainty” is actionable.


Treat your school calendar as authoritative. The IB communicates submission dates to schools, but schools normally set earlier internal deadlines for checking, authentication, and submission. This distinction is reflected in the IB’s information about[Extended Essay deadlines](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/extended-essay/submission-deadline/) and[TOK deadlines](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/upload-deadline/) .


### Prioritize by consequence, urgency, and uncertainty


Label each obligation **red** , **amber** , or **green** .


Priority Meaning Response


Red Due soon, incomplete, or blocking later work Protect a work block within 48 hours


Amber Important but not immediately due Set a milestone for this week


Green Submitted or progressing securely Maintain and review next week


An IA draft due in four days is red. A weak DP1 topic is usually amber unless a test is approaching. Uncertainty also raises priority, so if you do not understand an expectation or doubt whether an IA method is viable, ask the relevant teacher a precise question.


Limit yourself to **three major weekly priorities** . A practical combination is one coursework outcome, one subject weakness, and one administrative or university task. Other responsibilities receive shorter maintenance blocks.


### Build a September-to-November plan


### September: establish control


Confirm school deadlines and identify unfinished DP1 work. Move major coursework forward while using short retrieval sessions to revisit older formulas, concepts, vocabulary, or quotations.


Address structural problems early. If an EE research question remains too broad or an investigation lacks usable data, consult your supervisor instead of polishing weak material. RevisionDojo’s[Extended Essay guides](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ee-guides) can clarify structure and criteria, but your supervisor provides official school guidance.


### October: produce and diagnose


Create visible outputs: complete a section, process data, revise an argument, or apply feedback. For revision, attempt a short set of exam-style questions and classify each error as a knowledge, method, timing, interpretation, or command-term problem.


The[RevisionDojo IB Questionbank guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-question-bank-or-how-to-use-it-effectively) explains how to build a correction cycle rather than simply accumulating completed questions.


### November: stabilize before mocks


Reduce the number of unfinished major components and make exam practice more regular. Timed sections, essay plans, data-response questions, and mixed problem sets are often more manageable than frequent full papers while coursework remains active.


Identify the two or three weaknesses most likely to affect each subject. RevisionDojo’s[month-by-month DP2 guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/month-by-month-guide-ib-dp2) shows how preparation can develop beyond the fall term.


### Use a weekly system that survives busy days


A realistic week might include:


- **Daily:** 10-15 minutes of active recall
- **Four blocks:** 45-60 minutes for one defined output
- **One timed block:** 30-60 minutes of exam-style practice
- **One review block:** mark work, classify errors, and schedule a retest
- **One core block:** a specific EE, TOK, IA, or CAS action
- **One protected break:** time without an academic task


Adjust this structure to your timetable rather than forcing an ideal schedule that collapses after two days. The[RevisionDojo Study Planner](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/study-planner) can organize tasks around subjects and deadlines, but leave spare capacity for unexpected work.


End each week with a 15-minute review. Record what was completed, what caused delays, and which three outcomes matter next.


### Turn revision into evidence


Rereading notes feels reassuring but does not show what you can produce independently. Use a short active cycle:


1. Recall the concept without notes.
2. Check a concise explanation.
3. Answer an exam-style question.
4. Mark it honestly.
5. Record one specific error rule.
6. Retest the skill later.


Instead of writing “revise evaluation,” record an instruction such as “present supported strengths and limitations before reaching a justified judgment.” RevisionDojo’s[IB study features](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features) connect Study Notes, Flashcards, the Questionbank, and timed practice for this process.


### Handle coursework without chasing perfection


Work criterion by criterion, beginning with changes that improve reasoning, evidence, analysis, or methodology. Do not spend time perfecting formatting while a central argument remains weak.


Convert feedback into concrete actions. “Needs analysis” could become “explain the trend, discuss one limitation, and connect the result to the research question.” RevisionDojo’s[Coursework Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader) can offer rubric-informed feedback, but teacher instructions and permitted-feedback rules take priority.


Use Jojo AI to clarify concepts or question your reasoning, not to replace your authorship. The IB requires authentic student work, and AI-generated material included in assessed work must be acknowledged appropriately. Consult the IB’s[academic integrity guidance](https://www.ibo.org/about-the-ib/what-it-means-to-be-an-ib-student/responsibilities-of-students-and-ib-world-schools/academic-integrity/) and your school policy.


### Common mid-fall mistakes


Avoid these patterns:


- **Planning every hour:** Overfilled schedules cannot absorb fatigue or unexpected assignments.
- **Making everything urgent:** Priorities become meaningless.
- **Waiting for motivation:** Start with a 10-minute action that creates visible progress.
- **Sacrificing sleep:** Fatigue weakens concentration, recall, and judgment.
- **Practising without reviewing:** Improvement requires correction and retesting.
- **Hiding uncertainty:** Early questions prevent late emergencies.


If panic persistently disrupts sleep or ordinary functioning, speak to a trusted adult, counsellor, teacher, or DP coordinator. Planning can reduce uncertainty, but it does not replace appropriate wellbeing support.


### Conclusion


A successful DP2 mid-fall reset requires an accurate audit, three clear weekly priorities, concrete next actions, regular exam practice, and sufficient recovery. RevisionDojo can support this structure through the Study Planner, Study Notes, Flashcards, Questionbank, Jojo AI, and Coursework Grader. Start with the planner and one diagnostic question set, then let the evidence determine your next priority.
